::: {.callout-note title="Chapter overview"}
This chapter reads regression as prediction with quantified uncertainty.
It opens with the simple regression model, a straight line for the mean
of an outcome with three parameters, and reads those parameters in a
picture and in a simulated process whose values we know. It then turns
to a reported claim about education and income and a question about 102
occupations: we plot the records, fit a straight line, read its slope,
intercept, fitted values and residuals as a description of those
records, and see how least squares chooses the line and how well it
fits. Declaring the model for the occupations gives the slope a standard
error and an interval, repeated samples of the known process show what
the interval's coverage means, and prediction comes at three levels: a
point, a mean response and one new case. Checks of form, spread,
influence and support qualify these answers. The chapter closes with
regression toward the mean in its two versions, Galton's heights of
fathers and sons and a hypothetical class's two exams. By the end you
will be able to state and read a simple regression model, fit and read
one in R, say what its descriptive and model-based answers concern, and
recognize regression toward the mean in a before-and-after claim. An
appendix develops the mathematics.
:::

Suppose a report says, "Another year of education increases income by about
900 dollars." Before asking whether the number is significant, ask whose
education and whose income were measured: individuals, households and
occupations give three different comparisons.

\Needspace{6\baselineskip}

Our question is narrower:

> Among the 102 recorded Canadian occupations, how did occupation-average
> income differ across the supported range of occupation-average education in
> 1971, as summarized by a fitted straight line?

One row is an **occupation**, not a worker. An occupation with higher
average education need not contain the same people as one with lower
average education, so a comparison of their averages does not describe
what another year of schooling would do to one person's income.
Aggregate and individual relationships can differ substantially
[@robinson1950].

Regression can be read as **prediction with quantified uncertainty**.
A fitted line predicts an occupation's average income from its average
education; the residuals show how far each record lies from its
prediction; and, once a model for the records is declared, standard
errors and intervals say how uncertain the slope and the predictions
are. Section 1 states the model that gives a slope its meaning; Section
2 returns to the occupations.

{{< pagebreak >}}

## The Simple Regression Model {#sec-ch7-model}

### From a mean to a line

One common mean describes the centre of an outcome for all cases.
Allowing separate means for groups recognizes that different categories
may have different averages. Simple regression takes another step:
the mean changes continuously along a straight line as a numerical
predictor changes. The **conditional mean** is the mean outcome at a
stated predictor value.

For case $i$, write $x_i$ for its recorded predictor value and $Y_i$ for
an outcome the model could generate. We hold the complete set of
observed predictor values $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ fixed. Repetition means new
outcomes at those same values, so expectations and variances below
suppress conditioning on that fixed set. The mean and individual
outcome are

$$
E(Y_i)=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\qquad
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\varepsilon_i.
$$

The error $\varepsilon_i$ is how far case $i$'s outcome lies above or
below the true mean line. The conditions

$$
E(\varepsilon_i)=0,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i)=\sigma^2
$$

say that errors average zero at every recorded predictor value and
have the same variance everywhere. Two more conditions complete the
model used for exact inference. The errors are independent of one
another, a property of how cases were sampled, assigned or measured;
a good-looking plot cannot establish it. For the exact $t$ procedure
of Section 3 they are also Normal,
$\varepsilon_i\overset{\mathrm{ind}}\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)$.
Neither the distribution of the predictor values nor the pooled
outcomes needs to be Normal: the condition concerns errors around the
line at each predictor value. The predictor values must differ, since
points that all share one $x$ cannot determine a slope.

The model has three parameters: the **intercept** $\beta_0$, the
**slope** $\beta_1$ and the **error SD** $\sigma$. They belong to the
process that produces the data, and in practice they are unknown. A hat
marks a quantity computed from data: $\widehat\beta_0$ and
$\widehat\beta_1$ estimate $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$, and the residual SD
$s_e$ of Section 2.6 estimates $\sigma$.

### Reading the parameters

Regression is used to predict, and its parameters are read as
comparisons. @fig-ch7-model-parts draws each part of the model on six
invented points around the line $y=2+0.5x$.

Panel (a) shows the true line, the mean of $y$ at each $x$, with six
observed points around it. In panel (b) the slope, $\beta_1=0.5$, is the
difference in mean $y$ between cases one unit apart in $x$: two cases
that differ by one unit in $x$ have mean outcomes $\beta_1$ apart,
wherever they lie on the line. It compares different cases; it does not
say what would happen to one case whose $x$ changed. The intercept,
$\beta_0=2$, is the mean of $y$ at $x=0$, the baseline for these
comparisons. Reading it as a data-supported mean requires a meaningful
zero within the predictor's support, as in this illustration but not for
the occupations of Section 2.

In panel (c) each error $\varepsilon_i$ is the vertical distance from a

Under Normal errors about two-thirds of the outcomes lie within $\sigma$
of the line and about 95% within $2\sigma$. Here $\sigma=1$, and four of
the six invented points lie less than one unit from the line.

The line alone is a simple R graph; the surrounding scatter expresses
the separate assumption about errors.

### A process with known values

A simulation makes the model concrete. We choose the three parameters
ourselves, generate data from the model, fit a line and compare the
estimates with the values we chose. Take 20 predictor values equally
spaced from 6 to 16, close to the range of the occupations' education in
Section 2, and generate

$$
Y_i=2+0.5x_i+\varepsilon_i,\qquad
\varepsilon_i\overset{\mathrm{ind}}\sim\mathcal N(0,1).
$$

The true intercept is 2, the true slope 0.5 and the error SD 1; these
are a teaching construction, not records of any study.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(123)
known_data <- data.frame(x = seq(6, 16, length.out = 20))
known_data$y <- 2 + 0.5 * known_data$x + rnorm(20, sd = 1)
known_model <- lm(y ~ x, data = known_data)
```
:::


`set.seed()` fixes the random start, so the same 20 errors are drawn each
time, and `rnorm()` draws them with SD 1. `lm()` fits a straight line by
least squares, the rule of Section 2.4. @tbl-ch7-known-sample compares
its estimates with the known parameters.

## The Occupation Records and the Fitted Line {#sec-ch7-line}

We now return to the occupations of the opening question.

### The occupation records {#sec-ch7-question}

The data are distributed as *carData::Prestige* [@carData2022; @fox2019].
The package documentation attributes education and income to the *Census of
Canada* (1971), volume 3, part 6, pages 19-1 to 19-21. We treat that
documentation as a source record, not as evidence that the occupations
form a probability sample, and the calculations are our reanalysis.

| Feature | Meaning in this chapter |
|:--|:--|
| Unit and record count | 102 occupations; each occupation receives equal weight |
| Education, $x$ | Average years of education of occupational incumbents in 1971 |
| Income, $y$ | Average income of incumbents, divided by 1,000; thousand 1971 Canadian dollars |
| Missingness for the fit | No missing education or income values; no modeled rows excluded |
| Observed support | Education: 6.38--15.97 years; income: 0.611--25.879 thousand dollars |
| Descriptive estimand | Least-squares slope summarizing these 102 fixed occupation records |
| Limits of the source record | Cross-sectional and observational; no probability-sampling basis or individual-level analysis established here |

: Record, measurements, and scope for the focal analysis. {#tbl-ch7-record tbl-colwidths="[30,70]"}

Each occupation counts once, however many people it employs, so the
analysis does not describe an average worker's experience; and 1971
dollars are not today's purchasing power.

### Plot the records, then fit the line


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
prestige <- carData::Prestige
prestige$income_k <- prestige$income / 1000
library(ggplot2)
```
:::


The package-qualified name `carData::Prestige` selects the supplied
dataset, and dividing income by 1,000 changes its units without changing
any occupation.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(prestige, aes(education, income_k)) +
  geom_point(shape = 1, size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Average education (years)",
       y = "Average income (thousand 1971 dollars)")
```

### Fitted values, slope and residuals

A straight line assigns each observed predictor value $x_i$ a **fitted
value** $\widehat y_i$, the line's prediction for record $i$:

$$
\widehat y_i=\widehat\beta_0+\widehat\beta_1x_i,
\qquad e_i=y_i-\widehat y_i.
$$

The subscript $i$ indexes a record and the hat marks a fitted quantity.
The **residual** $e_i$ is observed minus fitted income: positive for an
occupation above the line, negative below it. It is computed from the
fitted line, unlike the error $\varepsilon_i$ of Section 1, measured from
the unknown true line.

For the occupation records, the line is

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{income}}=-2.8536+0.8988\,\mathrm{education}.
$$

With income in thousands of dollars, the slope says that fitted income
differs by 0.8988 thousand dollars, about 899 dollars, per one-year
difference in occupation-average education; a two-year difference
corresponds to $2\widehat\beta_1\approx1.7976$ thousand dollars.

For university teachers, the fitted coefficients before rounding give

$$
\widehat y=\widehat\beta_0+\widehat\beta_1(15.97)
\approx11.5005,\qquad
e=12.4800-\widehat y\approx0.9795,
$$

so their recorded income lies about 980 dollars above their prediction.
`predict()` applies the saved line to a record or to a new education
value without refitting:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
teacher <- prestige["university.teachers", ]
teacher_fit <- predict(model, teacher)
c(fitted = unname(teacher_fit),
  residual = teacher$income_k - unname(teacher_fit),
  at_12 = unname(predict(model, data.frame(education = 12))))
#>        fitted      residual         at_12 
#> 11.5004555017  0.9795444983  7.9321685196
```
:::


An occupation averaging 12 years of education has fitted income 7.9322
thousand dollars. @tbl-ch7-slope-readings sets the slope's reading
beside two sentences a report might also write about it.

| Another year of schooling raises a worker's income by about 899 dollars | One person before and after more schooling | No: it needs records of individuals and a causal design; occupation averages cannot supply either |

Only the first sentence compares what the records compare: occupations
that differ in average education. The second describes a change within
one occupation over time and the third a change within one person; the
records observe neither [@robinson1950]. The wording of a question
signals which reading it asks for. Words such as *difference*,
*relationship*, *higher*, *lower* and *predict* usually ask for a
comparison between units; *effect*, *impact*, *change*, *increase* and
*decrease* usually ask what a change would do, which needs a design that
supports it. The opening report, "another year of education increases
income", uses the second kind of wording for a comparison of the first
kind.

`lm()` returns this line whether or not Section 1's model holds for the

error and an interval answer a further question, which Section 3.1 asks
once the model is declared for the occupations.

### How least squares chooses the line

Ordinary least squares (**OLS**) chooses the intercept and slope that minimize
the **residual sum of squares**:

$$
RSS=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\widehat\beta_0-\widehat\beta_1x_i)^2.
$$

Squaring stops positive and negative residuals from cancelling and gives
large residuals more weight. "Best" means best by this criterion among
straight lines, not best for every research purpose. Two centered sums
give the solution:

$$
S_{xx}=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2,\qquad
S_{xy}=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y),
$$

$$
\widehat\beta_1=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}
=\frac{s_{xy}}{s_x^2}
=r\frac{s_y}{s_x},
\qquad
\widehat\beta_0=\bar y-\widehat\beta_1\bar x.
$$

Here $\bar x,\bar y$ are means, $s_x,s_y$ sample standard deviations,
$s_{xy}$ the sample covariance and $r$ Pearson's correlation. The
variance and covariance both divide by $n-1$, which cancels in their
ratio. The slope carries thousand dollars per education year; the
correlation has no units. For these data,

$$
\widehat\beta_1=\frac{675.8041}{751.8852}\approx0.8988,
\qquad
\widehat\beta_0=\bar y-\widehat\beta_1\bar x\approx-2.8536.
$$

The scalar covariance is $s_{xy}=6.6911$ thousand-dollar-years and
the education variance is $s_x^2=7.4444$ years squared. Dividing them
leaves thousand dollars per education year. Alternatively, the
unit-free correlation $r=.5776$ multiplied by the income SD over the
education SD restores the same slope and units. R applies both
identities directly to the recorded education and income values:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x <- prestige$education
y <- prestige$income_k
cov(x, y) / var(x)
cor(x, y) * sd(y) / sd(x)
```
:::


Both routes give 0.8988 using unrounded quantities from the same 102
complete pairs. This common set of records matters: separately
calculated summaries that omit different occupations need not
reproduce the fitted line.

A slope needs education to vary: if every occupation had the same
education, $S_{xx}=0$ and no slope could be identified. The line passes
through $(\bar x,\bar y)$, since substituting $\bar x$ into the intercept
formula gives $\bar y$. With an intercept, the residuals also sum to zero
and their products with $x$ sum to zero; otherwise the line could be
shifted or tilted to reduce RSS. These are algebraic properties of OLS,
not tests of independence or linearity. Because they tie the residuals
together, residuals are an imperfect window on the errors, which Section
6 keeps in mind. **Appendix A** derives them.

Three teaching records, $(x,y)=(1,2),(2,4),(3,3)$, show the whole
calculation at once. Their means are $\bar x=2$ and $\bar y=3$.
@tbl-ch7-tiny lays out the centered values, their squares and products,

The sums give $S_{xx}=2$ and $S_{xy}=1$, so

$$
\widehat\beta_1=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}=\frac12=0.5,\qquad
\widehat\beta_0=\bar y-\widehat\beta_1\bar x=3-0.5(2)=2.
$$

The fitted values 2.5, 3.0 and 3.5 lie on this line, the residuals sum
to zero, and their squares sum to $RSS=1.5$. No Normality assumption is
needed; the model of Section 1 enters only when we ask about
repeated-sample uncertainty.

### Candidate lines and centering

Least squares also lets us compare the fitted line with alternatives.
Make every candidate pass through $(\bar x,\bar y)$ and vary only its
slope $b_1$; then

$$
RSS(b_1)=RSS(\widehat\beta_1)
       +S_{xx}(b_1-\widehat\beta_1)^2.
$$

The added term is zero only at the OLS slope. @tbl-ch7-candidate-lines
and @fig-ch7-candidate-lines check five lines on the occupation records;
they are alternative summaries of the same records, not repeated samples.

### How well does the line fit? {#sec-ch7-fit}

A line can show a clear trend and still leave large differences between
occupations. For OLS with an intercept, the total variation of income
around its mean splits into two sums of squares:

$$
TSS=\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2=RegSS+RSS,
\qquad RegSS=\sum_i(\widehat y_i-\bar y)^2.
$$

For the occupation records, $1820.8134=607.4214+1213.3920$, in squared
thousand dollars. These are sums of squared deviations, not variances;
the split holds because the fitted deviations and the residuals have a
zero cross-product. The coefficient of determination is

$$
R^2=1-\frac{RSS}{TSS}
=1-\frac{1213.3920}{1820.8134}\approx.3336.
$$

The line accounts for a proportion .3336 of the squared variation of
income around its mean. "Accounts for" is algebraic: it does not mean
that education causes or determines income. With an intercept and one
predictor, $R^2=r^2$, here $.5776^2\approx.3336$.

The residual standard deviation, in thousand dollars, is

$$
s_e=\sqrt{\frac{RSS}{n-2}}
=\sqrt{\frac{1213.392}{100}}=3.4834.
$$

Fitting an intercept and a slope leaves $n-2$ residual degrees of
freedom. Under the model of Section 1.1, $s_e^2$ is an unbiased
estimate of the error variance and $s_e$ estimates the error SD $\sigma$
(Appendix A); without that model, $s_e$ measures residual scatter. It is
not the slope's standard error. `sigma()` returns it, and `summary()`
reports $R^2$:

## Inference for the Slope {#sec-ch7-inference}

### The slope's standard error and confidence interval

The slope 0.8988 is not waiting to be discovered: we computed it from all
102 records named in the question. A confidence interval answers a
further question, about a process that could generate new outcomes.
Apply the model of Section 1.1 to the occupations: suppose each
occupation's income arose independently from a process whose mean at
education $x_i$ is $\beta_0+\beta_1x_i$, with errors of common variance
$\sigma^2$, Normal for the exact $t$ procedure. The estimand is now
$\beta_1$, the slope of that hypothetical process, not the fixed slope of
the records, and repetition means new incomes at the same 102 education
values, not a new sample of occupations. Nothing in the records
establishes this process: it is declared, and its conditions are a
proposed justification that Section 6 examines.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}

The records depart from it: their spread grows with education, and the curve at 8 years reaches below zero income.](chapter_07_files/figure-html/fig-ch7-conditional-1.png){#fig-ch7-conditional fig-pos='H' fig-alt='The 102 occupation records and the fitted line rising from about 3 to 12 thousand dollars over education 6 to 16. :::
:::


@fig-ch7-conditional draws that model on the records, as panel (d) of
@fig-ch7-model-parts drew it on invented points, with the fitted line
and $s_e=3.4834$ in place of the unknown $\beta_0$, $\beta_1$ and
$\sigma$. The records do not look like that everywhere. At higher education they spread more widely, and
several incomes lie beyond the upper tails; at 8 years the curve reaches
below zero, a sign that a Normal model for a nonnegative outcome is an
approximation, which Section 5 meets again.

Substituting the process into the slope formula shows where slope
uncertainty comes from. The observed predictor values stay fixed, as in
Section 1.1, and $\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)=0$, so

$$
\widehat\beta_1-\beta_1
=\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)\varepsilon_i}{S_{xx}}.
$$

The fitted slope misses $\beta_1$ because the realized errors need not
cancel once weighted by distance from mean education. Independence and
common variance give

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\beta_1)
=\frac{\sigma^2\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}^2}
=\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}},
$$

which needs no Normality; Normality enters the exact $t$ reference.
Estimating $\sigma$ by $s_e$ gives the standard error and the 95%
interval:

$$
SE(\widehat\beta_1)=\frac{s_e}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}
=\frac{3.4834}{\sqrt{751.8852}}=0.127,
$$

The education values `x` defined in Section 2.4 give the same SE:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sigma(model) / sqrt(sum((x - mean(x))^2))
```
:::



$$
\widehat\beta_1\ \pm\ t_{.975,n-2}SE(\widehat\beta_1)
\approx0.8988\pm1.984(0.127)
\approx[0.6468,\ 1.1508].
$$

Here 1.984 is the 97.5th percentile of $t$ with 100 degrees of freedom.
More error variation raises the SE, and a wider predictor spread lowers
it. The test of $H_0:\beta_1=0$ gives
$t=\widehat\beta_1/SE(\widehat\beta_1)\approx7.0753$ and a two-sided
$p<.0001$: evidence against the zero-slope model under the stated
procedure. It is not the probability that the null is true, evidence of
causation or a measure of practical importance. The interval describes
what the procedure achieves over repetitions, which Section 4 makes
visible, not a 95% probability for the fixed parameter. The coefficient
table gives the estimate, SE and test, and `confint()` the interval, at
its default level .95:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

#>                  Estimate   Std. Error      t value        Pr(>|t|)

#> education    0.8988128418 0.1270354112  7.075293679 2.079192410e-10
confint(model, "education")
```

### The slope test and the correlation test {#ch07-correlation-test}

Chapter 5 tested a zero Pearson correlation. For an OLS line with an
intercept, fitted to the same complete pairs,

$$
\begin{aligned}
t_{\mathrm{slope}}
&=\frac{\widehat\beta_1}{s_e/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}
=r\sqrt{\frac{n-2}{1-r^2}}
=t_{\mathrm{Pearson}},\\
F_{\mathrm{regression}}
&=t_{\mathrm{slope}}^2
=\frac{R^2}{1-R^2}(n-2).
\end{aligned}
$$

The first identity follows from the covariance form of the slope and
$RSS=(1-r^2)TSS$; the second compares the intercept-only model with the
line, and squaring the signed $t$ gives the nondirectional $F$. For the
occupation line both $t$ statistics are 7.0753 on 100 df, and the $F$
statistic that `summary()` prints is $F(1,100)=50.0598=t^2$, all with
$p<.0001$. They are one comparison written three ways, not three pieces
of evidence.

The equality is algebra, and it needs the same intercept, rows, weights
and coefficient-covariance convention: a robust slope test of the kind
Section 6 introduces, which estimates the slope's SE without assuming
equal error variance, need not equal the ordinary $F$. For randomly sampled
bivariate-Normal pairs a zero population correlation, $\rho=0$, also
means a zero conditional-mean slope, but the occupation records have no
sampling warrant, so here the Pearson test only reproduces the process
calculation.

### A binary predictor and the two-sample t test {#ch07-binary-predictor}

## Prediction {#sec-ch7-prediction}

At a chosen fixed education value $x_0$ the line gives one number, which can
answer three questions of increasing uncertainty: what the line
predicts, what the mean income of occupations at $x_0$ is, and what one
new occupation's income will be. The last two need Section 1's model,
declared for the occupations in Section 3.1.

### Point prediction

The **point prediction** at $x_0$ is the fitted line's value,

$$
\widehat y_0=\widehat\beta_0+\widehat\beta_1x_0,
$$

built from the estimates, not the unknown parameters. At $x_0=12$ it is
7.9322 thousand dollars, the value `predict()` returned in Section 2.3.
By itself a point prediction says nothing about its uncertainty, and
the same number serves two different targets: it estimates the mean
income of occupations at $x_0$ and predicts one new occupation's income.

### The mean response and its confidence interval

Under the process model, occupations with education $x_0$ have mean
income $\mu_0=\beta_0+\beta_1x_0$, the **mean response**, a process
parameter. The point prediction estimates it, $\widehat\mu_0=\widehat y_0$,
with standard error

$$
SE(\widehat\mu_0)
=s_e\sqrt{\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}}
=3.4834\sqrt{\frac1{102}+
 \frac{(12-10.738)^2}{751.8852}}=0.3803
$$

at 12 years. The 95% **confidence interval for the mean response** is
$7.9322\pm1.984(0.3803)\approx[7.1776,\ 8.6868]$. The SE is smallest at
$\bar x$, grows with distance from it, and shrinks as independent records
accumulate: it describes uncertainty about an average, not the spread of
individual occupations. `predict()` returns the fit and the two limits:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
predict(model, data.frame(education = 12), interval = "confidence")
#>          fit        lwr         upr
#> 1 7.93216852 7.17757965 8.686757389
```
:::


### A new case and its prediction interval

One new occupation at $x_0$ has income $Y_0=\mu_0+\varepsilon_0$, a
random outcome with its own error. Predicting it by $\widehat\mu_0$ makes
an error with two parts,

$$
Y_0-\widehat\mu_0
=\varepsilon_0-(\widehat\mu_0-\mu_0),
$$

the new case's own error and the error in the estimated mean. When the
new error is independent of the fitted data and comes from the same
common-variance process, their variances add:

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y_0-\widehat\mu_0)
=\sigma^2+\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\mu_0).
$$

Substituting the mean-response variance and estimating $\sigma$ by $s_e$
gives

$$
SE_{\mathrm{new}}
=s_e\sqrt{1+\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}}
=3.5041,
$$

and the 95% **prediction interval**
$7.9322\pm1.984(3.5041)\approx[0.9802,\ 14.8842]$. The extra 1 is the new
outcome's own error variance, in units of $\sigma^2$; unlike the
mean-response SE, it does not shrink as the estimation sample grows.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
predict(model, data.frame(education = 12), interval = "prediction")
#>          fit          lwr        upr
#> 1 7.93216852 0.9801724429 14.8841646
```
:::

## Diagnostic Checks {#sec-ch7-check}

### Residuals, influence and unequal spread

The fitted line exists whether or not the model of Section 1.1 holds. Claims
that it describes a linear conditional mean, that its interval has the
stated coverage, or that it predicts new occupations well need more
support, and a check earns its place when its result could change one of
those claims.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Residual pattern and influence invite different follow-up questions.](chapter_07_files/figure-html/fig-ch7-checks-1.png){#fig-ch7-checks fig-pos='H' fig-alt='The left panel shows curvature and uneven scatter in residuals. The right panel shows Cook\'s distances, with physicians most influential for this fit.' width=614.4}
:::
:::


A curve in the residuals (@fig-ch7-checks, left) suggests that one
straight conditional mean leaves systematic variation, and a residual
spread that changes with the fitted value challenges the common-variance
SE. Leverage concerns an unusual predictor value; influence concerns how
much the fit changes when a record is left out. A large residual, high
leverage and high influence are related but different properties.

A minimal version of the first display plots residuals against fitted
values, with a horizontal reference at zero:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(fitted(model), resid(model))
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
```
:::


\Needspace{7\baselineskip}

For a straight line with an intercept, the leverage and Cook's distance
of record $i$ are

$$
h_i=\frac1n+\frac{(x_i-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}},
\qquad
D_i=\frac{e_i^2}{2s_e^2}\frac{h_i}{(1-h_i)^2}.
$$

Leverage grows with distance from $\bar x$; Cook's distance combines it
with the residual to summarize how far the fitted values move when record
$i$ is omitted (@fig-ch7-checks, right). It prompts a look at provenance
and a sensitivity analysis, not automatic deletion.

Adding education squared lets the fit bend. This same-record comparison
is an exploratory check, not a new final model:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
quad <- lm(income_k ~ education + I(education^2), data = prestige)
most <- which.max(cooks.distance(model))
without <- lm(income_k ~ education, data = prestige[-most, ])
c(full = unname(coef(model)[2]), without = unname(coef(without)[2]))
#>         full      without 
#> 0.8988128418 0.7982204353
coef(summary(quad))["I(education^2)", ]
#>       Estimate     Std. Error        t value       Pr(>|t|) 
#> 0.134179313419 0.047636405684 2.816738825952 0.005856544055
```

The curve is an exploratory sensitivity, not a selected final model.](chapter_07_files/figure-html/fig-ch7-curvature-1.png){#fig-ch7-curvature fig-pos='H' fig-alt='The quadratic fit bends upward toward higher education, unlike the constant-slope straight line. The quadratic coefficient, 0.1342, has $p=.0059$ under that model's

\Needspace{7\baselineskip}

An HC3 heteroskedasticity-consistent covariance gives a slope SE of
0.1491 rather than 0.1270 and, with the same $t_{100}$ multiplier, an
approximate interval $[0.6031,\ 1.1945]$. The line does not change. HC3
relaxes the equal-variance assumption for independent records; it does
not repair curvature, dependence, confounding or measurement error
[@white1980; @mackinnon1985; @long2000; @zeileis2004].

\Needspace{10\baselineskip}


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

c(classical = coef(summary(model))["education", "Std. Error"],
  HC3 = sqrt(V_hc3["education", "education"]))
#>    classical          HC3 
#> 0.1270354112 0.1490510028
```
:::


Later chapters go further: Chapter 8, Appendix B, builds the HC3 matrix
from its parts; Chapter 9, Appendix A, defines what a least-squares line
estimates when the conditional mean is not linear, and its Section 5.3
shows that measurement error in the predictor attenuates a slope. Nothing
here relies on them. @tbl-ch7-diagnostic-consequences collects the five
checks and what each can change.

\Needspace{20\baselineskip}

| Check | What needs to be examined | Consequence |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Form | Residual curve and a curved-fit comparison | A straight line may remain a description but fail as a constant conditional-mean slope account |
| Spread | Residual variation over fitted values | Classical SEs may need revision; HC3 is a variance sensitivity, not a universal repair |
| Influence | Source record and result with/without a consequential case | Disclose sensitivity; correct errors only when verified |

## Regression Toward the Mean {#sec-ch7-rtm}

**Regression toward the mean** first describes a simple line's
predictions. In standard units, with an imperfect correlation, its
prediction for a second measurement lies nearer its mean than the first
measurement lies to its own. Group averages follow that pattern when
the conditional mean is approximately linear; individual outcomes and
particular groups still vary around their predictions. The
phenomenon comes in two versions. In the first, two different but
related quantities are measured, such as a father's height and his
son's (Section 7.1). In the second, one quantity is measured twice, with
some luck in each measurement, such as a student's score on two exams
(Section 7.3). Either way the movement runs in both directions, as
Section 7.2 shows by selecting on the sons as well as on the fathers.

### Version one: fathers' and sons' heights

Francis Galton, who gave regression its name, noticed in the 1880s that
the grown children of tall parents were taller than average but, on
average, less tall than their parents, and the children of short
parents less short [@galton1886; @gelman2020]. He measured the adult
heights of parents and their grown children in 205 families. We use
James Hanley's transcription of Galton's notebook
[@hanley2004], distributed in the R package HistData [@friendly2025], and
keep one row per family: among the 179 families with at least one son,
one son was drawn at random from each, so every father appears once and
the rows describe separate families rather than brothers who share a
father. Heights are in inches, mostly recorded to the nearest half inch.
The small extract `galton1886_sons.csv` is
supplied with the chapter under this note: *Galton's family heights
(published 1886), transcribed by J. A. Hanley and distributed in the R
package HistData under the GPL; one son per family drawn for QMSBR. The
measurements are historical records in the public domain; the extract is
redistributed with this attribution.*

Fathers average 69.0989 inches and sons 69.2140. Written around the
fathers' mean, in the centred form of Section 2.5, the least-squares
line that predicts a son's height from his father's is

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{son}}=69.2140+0.4438\,(\mathrm{father}-69.0989).
$$

A father of average height is predicted to have a son of average
height, and each inch a father stands above or below the fathers' mean
predicts about 0.44 inch above or below the sons' mean. As in Section
2.3, the slope compares families: fathers an inch apart have sons
predicted 0.4438 inch apart. (The uncentred intercept, 38.5445 inches,
is the prediction for a father of zero height and places the line only.)
Because the two generations' SDs differ slightly, the general statement
uses standard units. Chapter 2 measured a value's distance from its mean
in standard units, $z_x=(x-\bar x)/s_x$, and Section 2.4 wrote the slope
as $\widehat\beta_1=r\,s_y/s_x$. Substituting that slope into the line
through the mean point, $\widehat y-\bar y=\widehat\beta_1(x-\bar x)$,
and dividing by $s_y$ gives the line in standard units:

$$
\frac{\widehat y-\bar y}{s_y}=r\,\frac{x-\bar x}{s_x},
\qquad\text{that is,}\qquad
\widehat z_y=r\,z_x .
$$

The line passes through the origin with slope $r$. Unless the
correlation is perfect, $\lvert r\rvert<1$, so a case $z_x$ SDs from the
mean on the predictor is predicted only $r\,z_x$ SDs from the mean on
the outcome. Galton called this regression toward mediocrity; we call it
regression toward the mean.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
galton <- read.csv("galton1886_sons.csv")
sapply(galton[c("father", "son")], sd)
#>      father         son 
#> 2.546555039 2.647465487
c(r = cor(galton$father, galton$son),
  z_slope = unname(coef(lm(scale(son) ~ scale(father),
    data = galton))[2]))
#>            r      z_slope 
#> 0.4269305719 0.4269305719
```
:::


`sapply()` applies `sd()` to both columns, and `scale()` converts a
column to standard units. The fathers' SD is 2.5466 inches and the
sons' 2.6475, and $r=.4269$. In inches the fitted slope is 0.4438 inch
of son's height per inch of father's height; in standard units it is
.4269, which is $r$. A father 1.6 SD above the fathers' mean
has a son predicted $.4269\times1.6=0.6831$ SD above the sons' mean:
taller than average, but less than half as far out.


::: {.cell}

The 24 fathers more than 1 SD above their mean average $z=1.6072$, or
73.1917 inches; their sons average 0.7029, or 71.0750 inches, close to
the line's prediction $.4269\times1.6072=0.6862$. The 30 short fathers
mirror them, and in every row the other height's mean lies between zero
and the selected mean, near $r$ times it. Selecting on the sons gives the
same movement backward in time: the 31 sons more than 1 SD above their
mean, at 1.4057, had fathers averaging only 0.6224. No force pulls
heights toward the average; a force could not act backward in time. The
imperfect correlation guarantees only that the line's predictions, in
standard units, lie nearer the mean than the values they are predicted
from. Groups follow those predictions on average when the mean of one
height is roughly a straight line in the other, as it is in these
families; even then each group's mean scatters around its prediction, so
no particular extreme group is guaranteed to sit nearer the mean.

If tall fathers have sons who are only tallish, and short fathers sons
who are only shortish, will each generation be more average than the
last, until after a few generations nearly everyone is about the same
height? That does not happen: the sons' SD, 2.6475 inches, is slightly
larger than the fathers', 2.5466. This is the **regression paradox**.
Its resolution is that a son's actual height is not his predicted
height: it is the prediction plus a part that his father's height does
not foresee, and that part adds spread back [@gelman2020]. The fitted
values carry the part of a son's height that his
father's height predicts, and spread only $r\,s_y=1.1303$ inches; the
residuals carry the rest, with spread $s_y\sqrt{1-r^2}=2.3941$ inches
(both SDs with the $n-1$ divisor; `sigma()` divides by $n-2$ and gives
2.4008). Variances add, not SDs: $1.1303^2+2.3941^2=2.6475^2$, which is
Section 2.6's decomposition divided by $n-1$, in which the fitted part
holds the share $R^2=r^2=.1823$. For this simple least-squares line,
the predicted standard-unit distances shrink by the factor $r$, while
the residual part keeps the outcomes more varied than their predictions.
In a stable population, one that keeps its
spread from generation to generation, the two parts balance
[@gelman2020]. Regression toward the mean describes predictions for
selected groups, not a population growing more uniform.

The two spreads can be compared directly. Fit the sons' heights to the
fathers' heights on the same records, then compare predictions with
observed heights:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
galton_fit <- lm(son ~ father, data = galton)
sd(fitted(galton_fit))
sd(galton$son)
```
:::


### Version two: one measurement taken twice

The second version measures one quantity twice, and an invented case
shows a mechanism behind it. Imagine a large class of 2,000 students
who sit a midterm and a final, with scores generated so that nothing
between the exams has any effect. Each student has a stable true score
$T_i$, and each exam adds luck independent of the true score and of the
other exam's luck, with the same error SD on both exams. This is the
true-score model of classical test theory that Part Two, Chapter 1,
develops:

$$
M_i=T_i+\varepsilon_{i1},\qquad F_i=T_i+\varepsilon_{i2},\qquad
T_i\sim\mathcal N(65,\,8^2),\qquad
\varepsilon_{i1},\,\varepsilon_{i2}\overset{\mathrm{ind}}\sim\mathcal N(0,\,6^2).
$$

Chapter 1 described reliability as the consistency of scores; here it is
the share of score variance that comes from the true score,
$8^2/(8^2+6^2)=.64$ on both exams. Only the true score repeats, so .64
is also the population correlation of the two exams, the slope of the line
in standard units that the sample $r$ estimates. The class is large so
that its group means carry little chance variation. The mathematics is
that of the heights, with the midterm in the father's place and the
final in the son's. Four lines of R generate the scores:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(12345)
true_score <- rnorm(2000, mean = 65, sd = 8)
midterm <- true_score + rnorm(2000, mean = 0, sd = 6)
final <- true_score + rnorm(2000, mean = 0, sd = 6)
```

### The regression fallacy

Regression toward the mean becomes a fallacy when the movement it
predicts is credited to a cause. Tversky and Kahneman [-@tversky1974]
recount a conversation with flight instructors: a trainee praised for an
unusually smooth landing tended to land less well next time, and a
trainee reprimanded for a rough landing tended to do better, so the
instructors concluded that praise hurts and criticism helps. As the
authors note, a teacher who misses regression toward the mean will
overrate criticism and underrate praise.

A quantitative understanding of prediction shows how this pattern can
arise without an effect of feedback. Suppose a landing reflects stable
skill plus independent luck on that attempt, as in the hypothetical
class. Landings that draw comment are selected for being extreme; a
later attempt is expected to be less extreme even if no feedback is
given [@gelman2020]. Crediting the whole movement to feedback without an
adequate comparison is the **regression fallacy**. Feedback could still
have an effect: the before-and-after pattern alone does not separate it
from regression toward the mean or other changes.

The fallacy compares what happened with a hidden benchmark: a second
measurement equal to the first, a son exactly as many SDs from his mean
as his father (the dashed line of @fig-ch7-rtm), a final score equal to
the midterm, a next landing as good as the last. That comparison assumes
perfect prediction. In the programmed exam example, the known
no-intervention mean is $65+.64(M-65)$, and its fitted line estimates
that relationship. For an actual intervention, the benchmark must be
the expected outcome **without the intervention**, supported by a
suitable design or credible untreated data. An arbitrary fitted line,
especially one fitted to outcomes already affected by feedback, cannot
supply that benchmark by itself. Exercise 5 states an earlier-year
no-tutoring relationship and asks what can be inferred if it also holds
for this year's pupils.

The same mechanism can matter when cases are selected for an extreme first
measurement and measured again: athletes and teams after a record
season, pupils chosen for low test scores and given extra help, patients
enrolled when their symptoms peak. Such
groups can move toward the mean even without an intervention under a
stable-score model with independent occasion errors. Random assignment
of help among similarly selected cases makes both groups subject to the
same selection mechanism, so their mean difference estimates the help's
effect under the design's conditions. A nonrandom comparison selected
and measured the same way also needs a justification that it represents
what would have happened without help [@barnett2005]. Chapter 14, Section 4.1,
applies this reasoning to selection on a noisy baseline.

## Reading Bridge {#sec-ch7-summary}

A simple regression starts from a model: the mean of an outcome is a
straight line in one predictor, with an intercept, a slope and an error
SD, and a process whose values we set shows estimates landing near
them, usually within about one SE. Applied to records, the line starts
with a unit and a comparison. Its fitted values are the line's
predictions for the records and its residuals the records' distances
from them; least squares puts the line through the mean point, with the
slope set by covariance and predictor variation. Across the 102
recorded occupations, fitted income rises by 0.8988 thousand 1971
Canadian dollars, about 899 dollars, per year of occupation-average
education over the observed 6.38--15.97 years: a bounded description of
the records, not an individual, causal or population return. Declaring
the model for the occupations gives the slope a standard error and an
interval, whose coverage repeated samples make visible. The residual
SD, $R^2$, the slope's standard error, and the mean-response and
new-case intervals answer different questions, and the checks say which
answers the records support. That is the chapter's through-line: the
line predicts, and, once a model is declared, standard errors and
intervals say how uncertain its slope and predictions are. In standard units
the line predicts $r$ times a case's distance from the mean, whether the
two measurements are a father's and a son's heights or one student's two
exam scores. Groups selected for extreme values are predicted nearer
the mean under the stated linear relation, while outcomes retain
residual variation. Reading a before-and-after gain as an effect needs
a credible no-intervention comparison and an appropriate causal design.
Argument Chapter A reads a short report of the occupation line as
an argument.

Chapter 8 writes the model with several predictors and reads a partial
slope, first on a simulated process with two predictors. On the
occupations it refits the education-only line on the 98 occupations
with a recorded type, so that the change from 102 to 98 records is not
mistaken for an effect of adjustment; it then adds prestige, percentage
of women and occupation type, and asks a separate held-out prediction
question. Chapter 9 takes Chapter 8's model as its map, changing its
mean part with factors of several levels, model comparison and changed
forms, and recomputing its uncertainty with robust and resampled
methods; its Section 7 (Project STAR) reads a randomized class-size
experiment whose uncertainty follows its school-clustered design
[@finn1990; @mosteller1995]. Chapter 10 extends the factorial interactions of
Chapters 4 and 6 to regression predictors.

### Key terms {.unnumbered}

Use this short reference to revisit the regression concepts introduced
here. The Part One Concept Reference gives the broader reference and the
principal home of each concept; fitted values, residuals, standard errors,
intervals, standardized values, and the reading vocabulary are explained
in Chapters 1--4.

| Term and common alternatives | Meaning |
|:--|:--|
| Simple linear regression (simple regression model; regression line) | A model in which an outcome's mean is a straight line in one predictor, $E(Y\mid x)=\beta_0+\beta_1x$, with errors around the line that average zero and share one SD $\sigma$; its three parameters are the intercept, the slope and $\sigma$. The least-squares line estimates the model's line: its descriptive use concerns the records fitted, and a model-based use needs a declared process. |
| Intercept | The fitted outcome at predictor value zero. It places the line vertically; when zero is outside the observed support, it is a mathematical anchor rather than a supported prediction. Centering the predictor moves it to a supported reference point. |
| Slope (regression coefficient) | The difference in fitted outcome per one-unit difference in the predictor, in outcome units per predictor unit. It compares units that differ in the predictor; it is not a change within one unit unless a design supports that reading. |
| Ordinary least squares (OLS) | The rule that chooses the intercept and slope minimizing the residual sum of squares. With an intercept, the fitted line passes through the mean point and the residuals sum to zero; the slope equals covariance divided by predictor variance. |
| Residual sum of squares (RSS) | The sum of squared residuals from a fitted line, in squared outcome units. Total squared variation about the mean splits into a regression part and RSS when the model has an intercept. |
| Residual standard deviation (residual standard error) | The square root of RSS divided by its residual degrees of freedom, in outcome units; with an intercept and one predictor the degrees of freedom are $n-2$. Under the process model it estimates the error SD. |
| R-squared (coefficient of determination) | One minus RSS divided by total squared variation: the proportion of centered squared outcome variation accounted for by the fit in these records. In simple regression with an intercept it equals the squared correlation. |
| Confidence interval for a mean response (mean-response interval) | An interval for the process mean outcome at a stated predictor value, using the SE of the fitted value. It concerns an average, narrows near the predictor mean, and does not cover individual outcomes. |
| Prediction interval (new-case interval) | An interval for one new outcome at a stated predictor value from the same process. Its variance adds the error variance to the fitted-mean variance, so it is wider than the mean-response interval and keeps a nonzero floor as the sample grows. |
| Leverage | A measure of how unusual a record's predictor value is relative to the others; it grows with distance from the predictor mean and appears in the SE of a fitted value and in influence measures. |
| Cook's distance (influence) | A summary of how much the fitted values change when one record is omitted, combining its residual and its leverage. It prompts inspection of provenance and a disclosed sensitivity, not automatic deletion. |
| Heteroskedasticity-consistent covariance (HC3; sandwich estimator) | A coefficient covariance estimate that allows unequal error variance across predictor values under independence. It changes SEs and intervals, not the fitted coefficients, and does not repair curvature, dependence, measurement error, or confounding. |
| Extrapolation (predictor support) | Using a fitted line at predictor values outside the observed range or where observations are sparse. Software returns a number there; the data do not support it. |
| Regression toward the mean (regression to the mean) | For a simple linear prediction in standard units, $\widehat z_y=r\,z_x$; when $\lvert r\rvert<1$, the predicted value is nearer its mean than the predictor is to its mean. In a stable repeated-measurement model with independent occasion errors, a group selected on an extreme noisy first score is expected to be less extreme on the second. These are statements about predictions or conditional averages, not every case; a narrower spread of predictions does not imply a narrower outcome distribution (the regression paradox). |
| Regression fallacy | Attributing to an intervention the movement expected from selection on an extreme noisy measurement. Evaluating an intervention requires a credible no-intervention benchmark, supplied by a suitable design or untreated comparison under stated assumptions; a fitted line through treated outcomes alone does not supply it. |

## Appendix A: Extended regression mathematics and interval derivations {.unnumbered #sec-ch7-app-a}

This appendix derives the identities the main text uses, keeping
identities about the observed records apart from claims about
hypothetical repetitions. Occupation calculations use the same 102 rows,
education in years and income in thousand 1971 Canadian dollars.

### Derivatives, normal equations, and the minimizing line {.unnumbered}

Start with a fitted model that predicts one common center $m$ for every
observation. Chapter 2 Section 2.2 states that the mean minimizes the
sum of squared deviations, and Chapter 3 Appendix A derives the identity
behind it:

$$
L(m)=\sum_i(y_i-m)^2
=\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2+n(m-\bar y)^2.
$$

Write $y_i-m=(y_i-\bar y)+(\bar y-m)$ and expand the square. The cross
term is zero because $\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)=0$. For $n>0$, the last term
is nonnegative and vanishes only at $m=\bar y$, so the mean uniquely
minimizes this criterion.

The three outcomes $2,4,3$ from Section 2.4 have mean 3 and
$L(m)=2+3(m-3)^2$, so their best constant line has loss 2. Letting the
fitted value depend on the three predictor values reduces RSS to 1.5,
as @tbl-ch7-tiny showed; neither result requires Normal errors or a
probability sample. Chapter 6's likelihood example chose a parameter by
optimizing a different criterion; here we develop the least-squares line
algebraically.

The intercept-and-slope criterion has two coefficients to determine, so
we set its two partial derivatives to zero and then verify that the
resulting line is the minimum. For candidate intercept $b_0$ and slope
$b_1$, define

$$
Q(b_0,b_1)=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-b_0-b_1x_i)^2.
$$

Differentiating with respect to each candidate coefficient gives

$$
\frac{\partial Q}{\partial b_0}
=-2\sum_i(y_i-b_0-b_1x_i),\qquad
\frac{\partial Q}{\partial b_1}
=-2\sum_i x_i(y_i-b_0-b_1x_i).
$$

At the minimum both derivatives are zero. The resulting **normal equations**
are

$$
n\widehat\beta_0+\widehat\beta_1\sum_i x_i=\sum_i y_i,
\qquad
\widehat\beta_0\sum_i x_i+\widehat\beta_1\sum_i x_i^2
=\sum_i x_iy_i.
$$

The first equation gives
$\widehat\beta_0=\bar y-\widehat\beta_1\bar x$.
Substitution into the second yields

$$
\widehat\beta_1
=\frac{\sum_i x_iy_i-n\bar x\bar y}
       {\sum_i x_i^2-n\bar x^2}
=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}.
$$

Here $S_{xx}=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2>0$ is required: a slope cannot be
identified when every predictor value is the same. Because sample covariance
and variance use the same denominator $n-1$,

$$
\widehat\beta_1
=\frac{s_{xy}}{s_x^2}
=r\frac{s_y}{s_x},
\qquad
\widehat\beta_0=\bar y-\widehat\beta_1\bar x.
$$

In the occupation data,

$$
\widehat\beta_1
=\frac{675.8041}{751.8852}\approx0.8988,
\qquad
\widehat\beta_0=\bar y-\widehat\beta_1\bar x\approx-2.8536.
$$

Unlike a correlation, the slope changes when a variable's units change.
Standardizing both variables makes their SDs one, so the slope becomes
$r$; Section 7 reads that line.

To verify that the stationary point is the unique minimum, write any other
line as $\widehat\beta_0+d_0+(\widehat\beta_1+d_1)x_i$. The normal
equations make the cross term with the OLS residuals vanish, leaving

$$
Q(\widehat\beta_0+d_0,\widehat\beta_1+d_1)
=RSS+n(d_0+d_1\bar x)^2+d_1^2S_{xx}.
$$

With $S_{xx}>0$, every different line has larger RSS. If a candidate line is
constrained to pass through $(\bar x,\bar y)$, its excess RSS is simply
$S_{xx}(b_1-\widehat\beta_1)^2$. Section 2.5 makes this
comparison visible with five candidate lines.

### Residual constraints and the decomposition of variation {.unnumbered}

At the OLS solution the derivative equations become
$\sum_i e_i=0$ and $\sum_i x_ie_i=0$. Thus the residuals have zero
sample covariance with the predictor and mean zero **by construction**.
They are not evidence that the unknown population errors are independent,
normally distributed, or conditionally mean zero.

The fitted line passes through $(\bar x,\bar y)$, so
$\widehat y_i-\bar y=\widehat\beta_1(x_i-\bar x)$. Its centred fitted
values therefore have zero cross-product with the residuals:

$$
\sum_i(\widehat y_i-\bar y)e_i
=\widehat\beta_1\left(\sum_i x_i e_i-\bar x\sum_i e_i\right)=0.
$$

Writing each observed deviation as its fitted part plus its residual,
then expanding the square, gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2
&=\sum_i\{(\widehat y_i-\bar y)+e_i\}^2\\
&=\sum_i(\widehat y_i-\bar y)^2+\sum_i e_i^2,
\end{aligned}
$$

since $\sum_i(\widehat y_i-\bar y)e_i=0$. This proves
$TSS=RegSS+RSS$, an algebraic decomposition of observed variation, not
a division into causal contributions. For these records,
$1820.8134=607.4214+1213.3920$, in squared thousand-dollar units.

Also $RegSS=\widehat\beta_1^2S_{xx}=S_{xy}^2/S_{xx}$. Dividing by
$TSS=S_{yy}$ proves $R^2=S_{xy}^2/(S_{xx}S_{yy})=r^2$ for simple
regression **with an intercept**. The identities need not hold for a
no-intercept fit. When fitted values are nonconstant,
$\operatorname{cor}(y,\widehat y)^2=R^2$ as well.

The two fitted coefficients impose the two residual constraints. Under
a correct linear mean with independent errors of common variance, the
same least-squares identity applied to the errors gives

$$
RSS=\sum_i\varepsilon_i^2-n\bar\varepsilon^2
-\frac{\{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)\varepsilon_i\}^2}{S_{xx}}.
$$

The expectations of the three terms are $n\sigma^2$, $\sigma^2$ and
$\sigma^2$. Thus $E(RSS)=(n-2)\sigma^2$, and $s_e^2=RSS/(n-2)$ is an
unbiased estimate of the error variance. Its square root $s_e$ estimates the
error SD in the outcome's units but is not itself exactly unbiased for
$\sigma$.

### From an error model to slope and intercept uncertainty {.unnumbered}

The 102-record least-squares line is already determined by those records.
The next derivations concern a **separate model-based question**: the
coefficients of a process that could generate new, independent
occupation outcomes at the observed education values. They assume the
model of Section 1.1 at fixed observed $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, with
$E(\varepsilon_i)=0$, $\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i)=\sigma^2$ and
$\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_i,\varepsilon_j)=0$ for $i\ne j$.
These are working conditions, not consequences of fitting `lm()`.
Section 3.1 derives the slope's variance, $\sigma^2/S_{xx}$, and its SE,
$s_e/\sqrt{S_{xx}}$. Because $\widehat\beta_0=\bar Y-\widehat\beta_1\bar x$ and
$\operatorname{Cov}(\bar Y,\widehat\beta_1)=0$,

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\beta_0)
=\sigma^2\left(\frac1n+\frac{\bar x^2}{S_{xx}}\right),
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat\beta_0,\widehat\beta_1)
=-\frac{\bar x\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}.
$$

Here $S_{xx}=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2$, as in Section 2.4. The covariance is
why simply adding the variances of an uncentered intercept and slope
would be wrong; with the predictor centered at its mean the two
estimates are uncorrelated, and the intercept SE is $s_e/\sqrt n$.

Under the stated linear-mean, uncorrelated, equal-variance conditions, OLS
is the best linear unbiased estimator: it has the smallest variance among
estimators linear in the outcomes and unbiased for the coefficients. This
Gauss--Markov statement does not require normal errors and does not establish
causal identification, valid measurement, or population coverage [@fox2016;
@kutner2005].

If the independent errors are also Normal, then
the standardized coefficient error is normal, $RSS/\sigma^2$ has a
$\chi^2_{n-2}$ distribution, and these quantities are independent. Their
ratio gives

$$
\frac{\widehat\beta_j-\beta_j}{SE(\widehat\beta_j)}
\sim t_{n-2},\qquad j=0,1.
$$

That is the basis of exact classical coverage for
$\widehat\beta_j\pm t_{.975,n-2}SE(\widehat\beta_j)$ and of the
corresponding null test, which Section 3.1 applies to the occupation
slope; the diagnostics of Section 6 do not support treating that
interval's nominal coverage as established.

These derivations condition on the predictor values, which need not have
been fixed by an experiment; a model with random predictors uses the same
conditional argument when its error conditions hold. Neither route shows
that the occupations were probability sampled, and neither requires
education or income to be Normal.

### Why a new-case interval has an additional variance term {.unnumbered}

For a supported value $x_0$, define the model mean
$\mu_0=\beta_0+\beta_1x_0$ and its estimate
$\widehat\mu_0=\widehat\beta_0+\widehat\beta_1x_0$.
Substituting the coefficient variances and covariance above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\mu_0)
&=\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\beta_0)
 +x_0^2\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\beta_1)
 +2x_0\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat\beta_0,\widehat\beta_1)\\
&=\sigma^2\left\{\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}\right\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

All predictor values, including the chosen $x_0$, remain fixed. A
confidence interval for this mean uses the square root with $s_e$ for
$\sigma$. A new occupation outcome is instead $Y_0=\mu_0+\varepsilon_0$;
if its error is independent of the fitted data and comes from the same
Normal, equal-variance process,

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y_0-\widehat\mu_0)
=\sigma^2\left\{1+\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}\right\}.
$$

The extra $1$ is new outcome variation, which would remain even if the
model mean were known. Both intervals use the same $t_{.975,n-2}$
multiplier. The table applies both formulas at four supported education
